paragraphs: Among the new things that drew my attention during my stay in the United States, none struck me more forcefully than the general equality of conditions. I soon saw the enormous influence this basic fact has on the whole course of society. It gives a certain direction to public opinion and a certain tone to the laws. It gives new maxims to those who govern and distinctive habits to those who are governed. I quickly realized that the influence of this fact reaches far beyond the country’s politics and laws. It has just as much power over civil society as over the government: it creates opinions, gives rise to feelings, suggests the ordinary practices of life, and changes whatever it does not itself produce. The further I went in studying American society, the more I saw that equality of conditions is the fundamental fact from which all others seem to follow, and the central point to which all my observations kept returning.

I then turned my thoughts to our own hemisphere, where I thought I could see something similar to the spectacle the New World had shown me. I observed that equality of conditions is advancing every day toward the extreme limits it seems to have reached in the United States, and that the democracy that governs the American communities is rising rapidly to power in Europe. That is how I came to conceive the book now before the reader.

Everyone can see that a great democratic revolution is under way among us, but people hold two opinions about its nature and consequences. Some regard it as a recent accident that can still be stopped. Others think it irresistible, because it is the most uniform, the most ancient, and the most lasting tendency in all of history. Consider the situation of France seven hundred years ago. The land was divided among a small number of families, who owned the soil and ruled the people living on it. The right to govern passed down with the family inheritance from generation to generation. Force was the only way one person could act on another, and landed property was the only source of power. Soon, however, the political power of the clergy arose and began to assert itself. The clergy opened its ranks to all classes, poor and rich, serf and lord. Equality entered the government through the Church, and a man who as a serf would have lived out his life in perpetual bondage took his place as a priest among nobles, often above the heads of kings.

As society gradually became more stable and more civilized, the relations among men grew more complicated and more numerous. People began to feel the need for civil laws, and the order of legal officials soon rose from the obscurity of the courts and their dusty chambers to appear at the monarch’s court, beside the feudal barons in their ermine and their mail. While kings were ruining themselves with their great enterprises and nobles were exhausting their resources in private wars, the lower orders were growing rich through commerce. The influence of money began to be felt in affairs of state. Business opened a new road to power, and the financier rose to a position of political influence in which he was both flattered and despised. Gradually, as learning spread and the taste for literature and art grew, talent gained chances of success. Science became a means of government, intelligence led to social power, and the man of letters took part in the affairs of state. The value placed on the privileges of birth fell in exact proportion as new paths to advancement opened. In the eleventh century nobility was beyond all price. In the thirteenth it could be bought. It was conferred for the first time in 1270, and so equality was introduced into the government by the aristocracy itself.

In the course of these seven hundred years, the nobles sometimes granted the people a share of political rights, either to resist the authority of the Crown or to weaken their rivals. More often, the king allowed the lower orders some measure of power in order to hold the aristocracy in check. In France the kings have always been the most active and the most constant levelers. When they were strong and ambitious, they spared no effort to raise the people to the level of the nobles. When they were moderate or weak, they let the people rise above themselves. Some helped democracy by their talents, others by their vices. Louis XI and Louis XIV reduced every rank beneath the throne to the same subjection. Louis XV, with his whole court, sank into the dust.

As soon as land came to be held on terms other than feudal tenure, and personal property in its turn began to confer influence and power, every improvement in commerce or manufacturing became a fresh element of the equality of conditions. From then on, every new discovery, every new want it created, and every new desire demanding satisfaction was a step toward a universal level. The taste for luxury, the love of war, the sway of fashion, and the most superficial as well as the deepest passions of the human heart all worked together to enrich the poor and impoverish the rich.

From the time when exercising the intellect became a source of strength and wealth, every addition to science, every fresh truth, and every new idea had to be seen as a seed of power placed within the people’s reach. Poetry, eloquence, memory, the grace of wit, the glow of imagination, the depth of thought, and all the gifts that Providence hands out with an equal hand turned to the advantage of democracy. Even when its adversaries possessed these gifts, they still served its cause by bringing out the natural greatness of man. Its conquests therefore spread along with those of civilization and knowledge, and literature became an arsenal where the poorest and the weakest could always find weapons ready to hand.

If we read through our history, we will hardly find a single great event in the past seven hundred years that has not turned to the advantage of equality. The Crusades and the English wars thinned out the nobles and divided their estates. The founding of communes introduced an element of democratic liberty into the heart of the feudal monarchy. The invention of firearms made the serf and the noble equal on the battlefield. Printing offered the same resources to the minds of all classes. The post was organized to bring the same information to the door of the poor man’s cottage and to the gate of the palace. Protestantism declared that all men are equally able to find the road to heaven. The discovery of America opened a thousand new paths to fortune and put riches and power within reach of the adventurous and the obscure. If we look at what has happened in France at intervals of fifty years, beginning with the eleventh century, we will invariably see a twofold revolution in the state of society. The noble has gone down the social ladder, and the commoner has gone up. One descends as the other rises. Every half century brings them closer together, and very soon they will meet.

Nor is this phenomenon at all peculiar to France. Wherever we turn our eyes, we see the same continual revolution throughout the whole of Christendom. In every country, the various events of national life have turned to the advantage of democracy. All men have helped it with their efforts: those who deliberately worked for its cause and those who served it without knowing it, those who fought for it and those who declared themselves its opponents. All have been driven along the same track and have worked toward the same end, some in ignorance and some unwillingly. All have been blind instruments in the hands of God.

The gradual development of the equality of conditions is therefore a providential fact, and it has all the characteristics of a divine decree. It is universal, it is lasting, it constantly escapes all human interference, and all events as well as all men contribute to its progress. Would it then be wise to imagine that a social movement dating from so far back can be stopped by the efforts of one generation? Is it believable that the democracy that has destroyed the feudal system and defeated kings will respect the citizen and the capitalist? Will it stop now that it has grown so strong and its adversaries so weak? No one can say where we are going, for we have nothing to compare with. Equality of conditions is more complete in the Christian countries of today than it has ever been at any time or in any part of the world. The extent of what already exists therefore prevents us from foreseeing what may still come.

This whole book has been written under the influence of a kind of religious dread, which the author felt as he contemplated a revolution so irresistible. It has advanced for centuries in spite of astonishing obstacles, and it is still going on in the midst of the ruins it has made. God does not need to speak himself for us to see the unmistakable signs of his will. We can discern them in the ordinary course of nature and in the constant tendency of events. I know, without any special revelation, that the planets move in the orbits traced by the Creator’s finger. Suppose the men of our time were led by careful observation and honest reflection to recognize that the gradual, progressive development of social equality is both the past and the future of their history. That single truth would give the change the sacred character of a divine decree. To try to stop democracy would then be to resist the will of God, and nations would have no choice but to make the best of the social lot Providence has assigned them.

The Christian nations of our age seem to me to present an alarming spectacle. The movement carrying them along is so strong that it cannot be stopped, but it is not yet so fast that it cannot be guided. Their fate is in their own hands, though in a little while it may no longer be. The first duty of those who direct our affairs at this time is to educate the democracy: to warm its faith, if that is possible; to purify its morals; to direct its energies; to replace its inexperience with a knowledge of practical affairs, and its blind impulses with an understanding of its true interests; to adapt its government to time and place; and to change it to suit the events and the people of the age. A new science of politics is needed for a new world. Yet this is what we think about least. Launched into the middle of a rapid stream, we stubbornly fix our eyes on the ruins still visible on the shore we have left, while the current sweeps us along and drives us backward toward the abyss.

In no country in Europe has the great social revolution I have been describing advanced as rapidly as in France, but there it has always been carried forward by chance. The heads of the state never planned for its demands, and its victories were won without their consent or without their knowledge. The most powerful, the most intelligent, and the most moral classes of the nation never tried to ally themselves with it in order to guide it. The people were therefore left to their wild impulses, and they grew up like those outcasts who are educated in the public streets and know nothing of society but its vices and its misery. The existence of a democracy seemed to be unknown, until it suddenly took possession of supreme power. Then everything was submitted to its whims, and it was worshipped as the idol of strength. At last, weakened by its own excesses, it was met by lawmakers who rashly conceived the plan of destroying its power instead of instructing it and correcting its vices. No one tried to prepare it to govern. Everyone set about shutting it out of the government.

The result has been that the democratic revolution has taken place only in the material parts of society, without the accompanying change in laws, ideas, customs, and manners that was needed to make such a revolution beneficial. We have gotten a democracy, but without the conditions that would reduce its vices and bring out its natural advantages. And although we already see the evils it brings, we do not know the benefits it may offer.

While the power of the Crown, supported by the aristocracy, governed the nations of Europe in peace, society had, amid its misery, several advantages that are now hard to appreciate or even imagine. The power of one part of his subjects was an insurmountable barrier to the prince’s tyranny. The monarch felt that the multitude saw him as almost divine, and the respect he inspired gave him a reason to use his power justly. However high they stood above the people, the nobles could not help taking the calm and kindly interest in its fate that a shepherd takes in his flock. Without acknowledging the poor as their equals, they watched over the destiny of those whose welfare Providence had entrusted to their care. The people had never conceived of a social condition different from their own, and they did not expect ever to rank with their chiefs. They accepted benefits from their superiors without questioning their rights. They grew attached to them when they were merciful and just, and they submitted to their exactions without resistance or servility, as to the unavoidable visitations of the arm of God. Custom and the manners of the time had also created a kind of law amid the violence and set certain limits to oppression. The noble never suspected that anyone would try to deprive him of the privileges he believed to be legitimate, and the serf regarded his own inferiority as a consequence of the unchangeable order of nature. It is therefore easy to imagine that a mutual exchange of goodwill took place between two classes so differently endowed by fate. Inequality and misery existed in society then, but the souls of neither class were degraded. Men are not corrupted by exercising power or debased by the habit of obeying. They are corrupted by exercising a power they believe to be illegitimate, and by obeying a rule they consider usurped and oppressive. On one side were wealth, strength, and leisure, along with the refinements of luxury, the elegance of taste, the pleasures of wit, and the religion of art. On the other were labor and a crude ignorance. Yet among this coarse and ignorant multitude it was not uncommon to find energetic passions, generous feelings, deep religious convictions, and independent virtues. A body politic organized in this way could boast of its stability, its power, and above all its glory.

But the scene has now changed. Gradually the two ranks are mingling. The divisions that once separated mankind are being lowered, property is being divided, power is shared, the light of intelligence is spreading, and the abilities of all classes are being cultivated equally. The state becomes democratic, and the empire of democracy is slowly and peacefully introduced into the institutions and manners of the nation. I can imagine a society in which all men would profess an equal attachment and respect for the laws, of which they are the common authors. The authority of the state would be respected as necessary, though not as divine, and the subject’s loyalty to the chief magistrate would be not a passion but a calm and rational conviction. Every individual would possess rights he is sure to keep, and a kind of manly confidence and mutual courtesy would arise among all classes, equally far from pride and from baseness. The people, well aware of their true interests, would accept that to enjoy the advantages of society they must meet its demands. In such a state of things, the voluntary association of citizens could take the place of the individual efforts of the nobles, and the community would be protected equally from anarchy and from oppression.

I admit that in a democratic state so constituted, society will not stand still. But the impulses of the social body can be regulated and directed forward. If there is less splendor than in the halls of an aristocracy, the contrast of misery will also be less frequent. The pleasures of enjoyment may be less extreme, but those of comfort will be more widely shared. The sciences may be less perfectly cultivated, but ignorance will be less common. The violence of feeling will be restrained, and the habits of the nation softened. There will be more vices and fewer crimes. Without enthusiasm or ardent faith, great sacrifices may be obtained from the members of a commonwealth by appealing to their understanding and their experience. Each individual will feel the same need to unite with his fellow citizens to protect his own weakness. Knowing that if they are to help him he must cooperate with them, he will readily see that his personal interest is the same as the interest of the community. The nation as a whole will be less brilliant, less glorious, and perhaps less strong. But the majority of citizens will enjoy greater prosperity, and the people will remain quiet, not because they despair of improvement but because they are aware of the advantages of their condition. Not all the consequences of this state of things would be good or useful, but society would at least have taken for itself all those that are. And having renounced the social advantages of aristocracy once and for all, mankind would enter into possession of all the benefits democracy can offer.

But here we may ask what we have adopted in place of the institutions, ideas, and customs of our forefathers that we have abandoned. The spell of royalty is broken, but it has not been replaced by the majesty of the laws. The people have learned to despise all authority, yet fear now extracts a larger tribute of obedience than reverence and love once did.

I see that we have destroyed the independent individuals who were able to face tyranny single-handed. But it is the government that has inherited the privileges taken from families, corporations, and individuals. The weakness of the whole community has therefore replaced the influence of a small body of citizens, which, if it was sometimes oppressive, was often conservative. The division of property has narrowed the distance between rich and poor. But it seems that the closer they come to each other, the greater their mutual hatred, and the more violent the envy and fear with which they resist each other’s claims to power. The notion of Right means nothing to either class, and Force gives both of them the only argument for the present and the only guarantee for the future. The poor man keeps the prejudices of his forefathers without their faith, and their ignorance without their virtues. He has adopted the doctrine of self-interest as the rule of his actions without understanding the science that governs it, and his egotism is no less blind than his devotion once was. If society is calm, it is not because it relies on its strength and well-being, but because it knows its weakness and its frailty. A single effort may cost it its life. Everyone feels the evil, but no one has the courage or energy to seek the cure. The desires, regrets, sorrows, and joys of the time produce nothing visible or lasting, like the passions of old men, which end in impotence.

We have, then, given up whatever advantages the old state of things offered, without receiving any compensation from our present condition. We have destroyed an aristocracy, and we seem inclined to look at its ruins with complacency and to make our home in the midst of them.

The state of the intellectual world is no less deplorable. The democracy of France, checked in its course or abandoned to its lawless passions, has overthrown whatever stood in its path and has shaken everything it has not destroyed. Its empire over society has not been introduced gradually or established peacefully. It has advanced constantly amid disorder and the turmoil of conflict. In the heat of the struggle, each partisan is carried beyond the limits of his own opinions by the opinions and excesses of his opponents. In the end he loses sight of the goal of his efforts and uses language that disguises his real feelings or secret instincts. Hence the strange confusion we are witnessing. I cannot recall a passage in history more worthy of sorrow and pity than the scenes taking place before our eyes. It is as if the natural bond that joins a man’s opinions to his tastes and his actions to his principles had now been broken. The sympathy that has always been recognized between human feelings and ideas seems to have dissolved, and all the laws of moral analogy seem to have been abolished.

There are zealous Christians among us whose minds are nourished by the love and knowledge of a future life, and who readily take up the cause of human liberty as the source of all moral greatness. Christianity, which has declared all men equal in the sight of God, will not refuse to acknowledge that all citizens are equal in the eyes of the law. But by an odd concurrence of events, religion has become entangled in those institutions that democracy attacks. It is not infrequently driven to reject the equality it loves, and to curse as an enemy the cause of liberty, which it might hallow by its alliance.

Beside these religious men I see others whose eyes are turned more toward the earth than toward Heaven. They support liberty not only as the source of the noblest virtues but especially as the root of all solid advantages, and they sincerely want to extend its sway and bring its blessings to mankind. It would be natural for them to hurry to call on religion for help, for they must know that liberty cannot be established without morality, nor morality without faith. But they have seen religion in the ranks of their adversaries, and they inquire no further. Some of them attack it openly, and the rest are afraid to defend it.

In earlier ages, slavery was defended by the venal and the servile-minded, while the independent and the warm-hearted struggled without hope to save the liberties of mankind. But today we meet men of high and generous character whose opinions contradict their inclinations, and who praise a servility they have never known themselves. Others, on the contrary, speak in the name of liberty as if they could feel its sanctity and its majesty, and loudly claim for humanity rights that they have always denied. There are virtuous and peaceable people whose pure morality, quiet habits, affluence, and talents fit them to be the leaders of those around them. Their love of country is sincere, and they are ready to make the greatest sacrifices for its welfare. But they confuse the abuses of civilization with its benefits, and in their minds the idea of evil cannot be separated from that of novelty.

Not far from this class is another party, whose aim is to make mankind materialistic: to find what is expedient without regard for what is just, to gain knowledge without faith, and prosperity apart from virtue. They take the title of champions of modern civilization and put themselves in a position that they insolently usurp and from which their own unworthiness drives them. Where are we, then? The religious are the enemies of liberty, and the friends of liberty attack religion. The high-minded and noble advocate subjection, and the meanest and most servile minds preach independence. Honest and educated citizens oppose all progress, while men without patriotism or principles are the apostles of civilization and intelligence. Has this been the fate of the centuries before ours? Has man always lived in a world like the present one, where nothing is linked together, where virtue lacks genius and genius lacks honor, where the love of order is confused with a taste for oppression and the sacred rites of freedom with contempt for law? Is it a world where the light conscience casts on human actions is dim, and where nothing seems any longer forbidden or allowed, honorable or shameful, false or true? I cannot believe, however, that the Creator made man in order to leave him in an endless struggle with the intellectual miseries that surround us. God has a calmer and more certain future in store for the communities of Europe. I do not know his designs, but I will not stop believing in them because I cannot fathom them. I would rather doubt my own understanding than his justice.

There is one country in the world where the great revolution I am speaking of seems to have nearly reached its natural limits. It has been carried out there with ease and simplicity. Or rather, that country has arrived at the consequences of the democratic revolution we are going through without having experienced the revolution itself. The emigrants who settled on the shores of America at the beginning of the seventeenth century separated the democratic principle from all the principles that held it back in the old communities of Europe, and they transplanted it, unmixed, to the New World. There it has been allowed to grow in perfect freedom and to bring out its consequences in the laws by shaping the manners of the country.

It seems to me beyond doubt that sooner or later we will arrive, like the Americans, at an almost complete equality of conditions. But I do not conclude from this that we will necessarily be led to draw the same political consequences that the Americans have drawn from a similar social organization. I am far from supposing that they have chosen the only form of government a democracy can adopt. But the fact that the same underlying cause shapes laws and manners in both countries is enough to explain why we have such an immense interest in knowing its effects in each of them.

It is not, then, merely to satisfy a legitimate curiosity that I have examined America. I wanted to find lessons from which we can ourselves profit. Anyone who imagines that I meant to write a panegyric will see that this was not my purpose. Nor have I tried to argue for any particular form of government, for I believe that absolute excellence is rarely to be found in any legislation. I have not even pretended to discuss whether the social revolution, which I believe to be irresistible, is good or bad for mankind. I have accepted this revolution as a fact already accomplished or on the eve of being accomplished. Among the nations that have undergone it, I chose the one in which its development has been the most peaceful and the most complete, so that I could discern its natural consequences and, if possible, identify the means by which it can be made profitable. I confess that in America I saw more than America. I looked for the image of democracy itself, with its inclinations, its character, its prejudices, and its passions, in order to learn what we have to fear or hope from its progress.

In the first part of this work I have tried to show the tendency that the democracy of America gives to the laws. That democracy is left almost without restraint to its instinctive impulses. I have also tried to show the course it prescribes for the government and the influence it has on public affairs. I have sought to discover the evils and the advantages it produces. I have examined the precautions the Americans take to direct it, and those they have not taken, and I have undertaken to point out the causes that enable it to govern society. I do not know whether I have succeeded in making known what I saw in America. But I am certain that this has been my sincere desire, and that I have never knowingly bent facts to fit ideas instead of ideas to fit facts.

Whenever a point could be established from written documents, I went to the original text and to the most authentic and respected works. I have cited my authorities in the notes, and anyone may consult them. Whenever the question concerned an opinion, a political custom, or a remark about the manners of the country, I tried to consult the best-informed men I met. If the point was important or doubtful, I was not satisfied with one witness, but formed my opinion from the testimony of several. Here the reader must necessarily take my word. I could often have named people he knows, or who deserve to be known, as proof of what I say, but I have carefully avoided doing so. A stranger often hears important truths at his host’s fireside that the host would perhaps hide from the ear of a friend. The host consoles himself with his guest for the silence he is otherwise bound to keep, and the shortness of the traveler’s stay removes any fear that he will be indiscreet. I carefully noted down every conversation of this kind as soon as it happened, but these notes will never leave my writing case. I would rather weaken the force of my statements than add my name to the list of strangers who repay generous hospitality with later vexation and annoyance.

I know that, in spite of my care, nothing will be easier than to criticize this book, if anyone ever chooses to. Readers who examine it closely will discover the fundamental idea that connects its several parts. But the subjects I have had to treat are extremely diverse, and it will not be difficult to set an isolated fact against the body of facts I cite, or an isolated idea against the body of ideas I put forward. I hope to be read in the spirit that has guided my work, and I hope my book will be judged by the general impression it leaves, just as I formed my own judgment not on any single reason but on the mass of evidence. We must not forget that an author who wants to be understood is obliged to push all his ideas to their furthest theoretical consequences, often to the verge of what is false or impractical. In active life we sometimes have to depart from the rules of logic, but this is not so in discourse, and a man finds that nearly as many difficulties come from inconsistency of language as usually come from inconsistency of conduct.

I conclude by pointing out myself what many readers will consider the main defect of the work. This book is written to favor no particular views, and in composing it I have had no intention of serving or attacking any party. I have tried not to see differently from them but to look further than they do. While they are busy with tomorrow, I have turned my thoughts to the Future.
